summary: Describes subprograms at the University of California, Santa Barbara that let PL/I programs on the IBM 360/75 use the ARPANET. Like its Fortran counterpart in RFC 119, it provides an interface to the local Network Control Program, with a completion code variable tracking each socket that is not closed.

plainLanguage.summary: A helper standing between a PL/I program and the network, passing messages back and forth. It does the same job as the Fortran version, but for a different programming language.

subtitle: Subprograms that let PL/I programs on a UCSB IBM 360/75 open sockets and move data over the early ARPANET.

tldr.problem: Programmers at UCSB wanted to use the ARPANET from PL/I programs, but the Network Control Program (NCP) was not directly callable from that language.
tldr.mechanism: A set of assembly-language subprograms such as OPEN, CLOSE, SEND, RECEIVE and CHECK wraps the NCP. Each socket is tracked by a completion code variable that receives a numeric result.
tldr.outcome: PL/I programs compiled at UCSB can make connections, transfer data and drive the On-Line System display. The library is specific to that one site.

today: RFC 120 describes a library for one site's 1971 system, and its status is listed as Unknown. It has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Calling the Network from PL/I
sections.content:
Mark Krilanovich of UCSB describes subroutines, written in assembly language, that make the Network accessible through the NCP to PL/I programs running on the 360/75. They can be called from any PL/I main program or subroutine compiled at UCSB.

Each socket that is not closed has a completion code variable, which identifies the local socket and receives a code describing the outcome. It must be BINARY FIXED(31,0)ALIGNED. Most calls wait without using CPU time until the NCP reports completion, bounded by a time limit given in tenths of a second. If the limit is exceeded, code 252 is returned and the operation stays pending.
sections.plainLanguage: Each open line gets a little mailbox variable. After every action, the helper puts a number in it that says how it went.

sections.title: Connections: OPEN and CLOSE
sections.content:
A socket is named by a two-element array: the site number, then the socket number. A socket's gender is even or odd by its absolute value.

OPEN does three jobs. CONNECT links a local socket to a foreign one and waits for acceptance or rejection. LISTEN waits for a call to a local socket and returns the caller's socket identifier. ACCEPT accepts the connection from the last successful LISTEN. All three need the socket to be in the closed state, except ACCEPT, which needs the last operation to have been a LISTEN.

CLOSE returns a socket to the closed state. It refuses a pending LISTEN, aborts a CONNECT, and on an open connection lets data in transit reach the foreign socket first. Completion code 0 always means success; for example, 20 on CONNECT means the foreign process rejected the attempt.
sections.plainLanguage: Opening is like dialing a friend, waiting for someone to pick up, or answering the phone. Closing is hanging up politely after the last words get through.

sections.title: Moving Data and Checking Status
sections.content:
SEND (entry WRITE) and RECEIVE (entry READ) move data measured in bits, starting at an optional bit offset in the buffer. A non-positive length does nothing. Completion codes cover a wrong socket gender, a transfer already in progress, a connection that is not fully open, and a peer that closed early.

CHECK reports a socket's status at any time without a completion code. It returns a number, an eight-byte mnemonic, the foreign socket and a bit deficit. Status values run from 0 (OPEN) and 1 (LISTEN) through 6 (CLOSED) to 10 (DRAIN-->).

IDENTIFY maps a completion code variable back to its socket. SIGNAL conveys a user-defined signal, so that the foreign side's next SEND or RECEIVE is suppressed with a code saying a signal arrived.
sections.plainLanguage: Sending and receiving are like pouring water through a pipe and counting the cups. Checking is peeking to see whether the pipe is open, closed or still draining.

sections.title: On-Line System Console Messages
sections.content:
Several subprograms suit the On-Line System network operators. Data travels in messages of three fields: a one-byte op code, a two-byte length in bits, and the text. The op code and length together are the header. A final header with a NOP op code is the trailer.

Op code 0 is a NOP, 1 carries EBCDIC characters for immediate display, 2 carries key codes for immediate execution, and 3 carries key codes whose execution waits until all data for the receive operation has arrived.

WTOLC writes characters to the console with a shift level and a position across and down. RFOLC reads them back, and WTOLCR writes then waits for a reply. ERASE sends a command to erase the display.
sections.plainLanguage: Each note to the screen has a label saying what it is, how long it is, and then the words. A special empty note says the message is over.

items.label: NOP
items.desc: No text field; mainly used as a delimiter and as the trailer.

items.label: EBCDIC text
items.desc: Characters, one per byte, displayed as soon as received.

items.label: Key pushes
items.desc: One byte per key, executed as soon as received.

items.label: Delayed key pushes
items.desc: Like 2, but execution waits until all data for the receive operation has arrived.

references.text: Fortran counterpart of the Network subprograms, RFC 119.
